title: Tesla confirms September 3 Cybercab launch event in Austin, invites go out
subtitle: Tesla sent formal invitations for a Sept. 3 event where select riders will get first access to its two-seat, steering-wheel-free Cybercab robotaxi.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Tesla confirmed on August 23 that it will launch the Cybercab on September 3 at an invitation-only event in Austin, Texas. The company sent formal invites over the weekend and told riders who completed trips in its existing Model Y robotaxi fleet through August 23 that they were entered in a sweepstakes for exclusive access. Winners will be notified on August 25. The Cybercab is Tesla's first purpose-built ride-sharing vehicle — two seats, no steering wheel, no pedals — and it will run on Tesla's AI4 compute platform alongside the Model Ys already driving passengers in Austin and, as of last week, Las Vegas.

The date matters because the Cybercab has been on and off the calendar since Tesla first unveiled it in October 2024, when Elon Musk said production would begin before 2027 at a target price under $30,000. A confirmed public event with rides — rather than another stage demo — is the point at which the promise turns into a fleet a regulator can inspect. Nevada's approval last week to deploy up to 5,000 Tesla robotaxis in Clark County over the next 12 months set up the September event as the moment Tesla starts operating a car with no manual controls in real traffic.

The launch lands into a robotaxi market that is finally competitive. Waymo now runs paid rides in 11 U.S. cities and got the same Nevada permit Tesla did. Zoox is expanding in Las Vegas. Uber is bundling autonomous rides across all three networks. What differentiates the Cybercab is the vehicle itself: purpose-built for autonomy at a price that, if Tesla hits it, undercuts every existing robotaxi platform on capital cost per seat-mile. Whether the software is ready for a car with no fallback controls is what September 3 will test.

A note for learners: watch what riders can and can't do at the event. A steering-wheel-free vehicle is a regulatory statement as much as an engineering one — it removes the human takeover path that every other L4 program still keeps in reserve. The specific route geometry Tesla picks, whether a safety driver is present in a chase car, and how the fleet handles construction zones will tell you more about the state of the software than any keynote number.
